findings.finding: 19% of US online shoppers abandoned a checkout in the prior 3 months because they did not trust the site with their credit card information.
findings.quote: In fact, our most recent Checkout Usability study reveals that 19% of users have abandoned a checkout flow during the last 3 months because they “ didn’t trust the site with their credit card information” (1,026 respondents, average US adult internet population, 2025).
findings.context: Baymard's 2025 quantitative Checkout Usability survey of the average US adult internet population, 1,026 respondents, asking why they abandoned a checkout in the last 3 months.
findings.caveat: Ecommerce checkout, where money changes hands; our app is free, so the exposure is smaller. Self-reported abandonment reasons, not an A/B test of any reassurance line.
findings.implication: Reading it the other way, a visitor with no payment risk still carries a trust reflex, so say 'free, no card' next to the button instead of leaving her to assume it.

findings.finding: Replacing a forced-registration form with a 'You do not need to create an account' message and a plain Continue button raised the number of customers purchasing by 45% at one large retailer.
findings.quote: The number of customers purchasing went up by 45%.
findings.context: One $25-billion retailer; the old form had Login / Register; the new Continue button carried the message 'You do not need to create an account to make purchases on our site... you can create an account during checkout.' Before/after on live traffic. No sample size is printed on the page.
findings.caveat: Single case study from a UX consultancy, a redesign (button + message together), an old retail site, written by the UX consultant who ran the usability tests; no confidence interval. Retail checkout, not a free quiz.
findings.implication: If the app asks for an email or account before she sees her board, either remove that ask or say 'no account needed to see your board' right at the button.

findings.finding: The longer the stated length of a web survey, the fewer people started it: 75% started when told 10 minutes, 65% at 20 minutes, 62% at 30 minutes.
findings.source_name: Survey Research Methods 2025 (Hanson et al.), citing Galesic & Bosnjak 2009
findings.quote: Their findings revealed that 75% started the 10-minute survey, compared with 65% for the 20-minute survey and 62% for the 30-minute survey.
findings.context: Galesic & Bosnjak (Public Opinion Quarterly 2009) announced to respondents of an opt-in web survey in Croatia that it would take 10, 20 or 30 minutes; this open-access 2025 paper reports their starting rates.
findings.caveat: SECONDHAND mention of the 2009 paper (the original is paywalled; numbers not checked against it). Minutes, not seconds; a survey, not a signup. The same 2025 paper's own experiment found only a small response-rate gain from a shorter questionnaire, so the effect shrinks.
findings.implication: This is the only time-label evidence found: the stated duration changes who starts. Print the true duration ('about 90 seconds', 'tap 10 photos') next to the button, and test it.

findings.finding: An A/B test that added six reassurances (the product 'does not spy on people') to a home page raised paid account signups by a possible +17%.
findings.quote: Here is another really interesting A/B test where six reassurances were used (among a handful of other changes) to drive paid account signups by a possible +17% right from a home page.
findings.context: covenanteyes.com, 4 variations, test ran 'just over a month'; the page gives no visitor counts or significance (the full data is paywalled in GoodUI Issue #20).
findings.caveat: Weak: the six reassurances were bundled with 'a handful of other changes'; the page says 'possible'; privacy-sensitive product; paid signups, not a free action; no sample size on the page.
findings.implication: Reassurance copy near the ask is plausible to help, but nobody can say how much from this test; use it as a reason to run our own test, not as a forecast.

findings.finding: Replacing a passive video with an interactive reassurance that tailored itself to the visitor's specific need raised sale starts by 20%, with a possible +12% into first-time sales.
findings.quote: Reassuring gradually showed an increase of 20% to sale starts (visits to next page), with a possible +12% follow through into First Time Sales (visits to post-purchase page for new customers).
findings.context: wpallimport.com home page; tests ran for 5 months; interactive 'gradual reassurance' replaced a video; the page gives no visitor counts.
findings.caveat: Single site, vendor-reported by the test consultant, no sample size on the page; the +12% is labelled 'possible'; B2B software.
findings.implication: Evidence (weak) that an interactive element that shows the visitor something tailored to her can beat a passive explainer; supports a clickable preview of the board over a static picture or video.

findings.finding: Across GoodUI's database, only 169 of about 650 published A/B tests of its UI patterns were winning tests; 285 were insignificant positives, about 150 insignificant negatives and 43 losing tests.
findings.quote: 285 insignificant positive tests 169 winning tests
findings.context: GoodUI aggregates tests from trusted companies on 141 UI patterns; its Patterns page said '141 patterns based on 647 tests' when read and 648 minutes later, so the counts change as tests are added (43 losing tests, about 150 insignificant negative tests, 285 insignificant positive tests, 169 winning tests).
findings.caveat: Self-reported, voluntarily shared tests; not specific to wedding or free-app CTAs. Used here only as a calibration of how often a plausible tweak actually wins.
findings.implication: Treat every cue in this file (reassurance lines, time labels, previews) as a hypothesis: about one test in four wins clearly, so ship one change at a time and measure clicks.

findings.finding: In a field experiment, when the cheaper chocolate went from 1 cent to free, its share of choices jumped from 27% to 69%, far more than a 1-cent price cut should explain.
findings.source_name: Shampanier, Mazar & Ariely, Marketing Science 2007 (Duke-hosted PDF)
findings.quote: 27% in the 1&15 condition to 69% in the 0&14
findings.context: Experiment 2 (real purchases at a booth in MIT's student center): Hershey's Kiss vs Lindt truffle, prices 1 cent / 15 cents versus free / 14 cents; the quoted shares exclude those who took nothing. The page prints degrees of freedom above 260 but not a headcount.
findings.caveat: Product-pricing study with students buying real chocolate, not a web CTA; the quote is a fragment because the PDF has two columns and pdftotext interleaves them. Whether the word 'free' on a button has this pull is not tested.
findings.implication: A zero price is treated differently from a tiny price, so the word 'free' should be explicit on the button and the line beside it, not implied.

findings.finding: On HubSpot's blog, plain end-of-post banner CTAs produced about 6% of a post's leads, while the in-text anchor CTA alone produced up to 93%.
findings.quote: In HubSpot‘s limited test of 10 blog posts, regular end-of-post banner CTAs contributed an average of just 6% of leads that the blog posts generated, whereas up to 93% of a post’s leads came from the anchor-text CTA alone.
findings.context: HubSpot's own 'limited test of 10 blog posts' comparing end-of-post banner CTAs with a standalone line of text linked to a landing page, styled as an H3 or H4, placed inside the post.
findings.caveat: Vendor (HubSpot), 'limited test', only 10 posts, observational share-of-leads (not a randomised A/B), blog-to-lead-form not blog-to-app; the 93% is the best post, not the average.
findings.implication: Put the main link as a sentence-style text CTA inside the answer, at the point where she has just got her number, not only a banner after the last paragraph.

findings.finding: HubSpot reports that personalized CTAs converted 202% better than basic CTAs across 330,000+ CTAs over six months.
findings.quote: After analyzing and comparing more than 330,000 CTAs over a six-month timeframe, we discovered that personalized CTAs convert 202% better than basic CTAs.
findings.context: HubSpot's own comparison of CTAs on its platform: personalized (targeted to the visitor, e.g. lifecycle stage) vs basic (same for everyone).
findings.caveat: Vendor claim selling a CTA tool; observational, no control or sample breakdown printed; 'personalized' means per-visitor targeting, not 'matches the page topic', so it is only indirect support for content-matched CTAs.
findings.implication: Targeting the offer to the visitor beats a one-size button; on a static page the closest thing is wording the button around the page's topic ('see dresses like this under $500').

findings.finding: Adding a post-specific checklist offer (a 'content upgrade') with two links in the body of one blog post lifted that post's opt-in rate from 0.54% to 4.82%.
findings.quote: The result? A 785% increase in conversions (compared to the previous month).
findings.context: One high-traffic post ('Google's 200 Ranking Factors'); links at the top and bottom; over 4700 unique visitors and 370 conversions on that page after the change; the author says the blog had a grand total of 54 opt-in forms.
findings.caveat: Before/after versus the previous month, not an A/B test; one post, 2016, a vendor-blogger's own result; the gain is email opt-in for a freebie specific to the post, not a click into a tool.
findings.implication: An offer that is specific to the page the reader is on (a board for THIS city's courthouse weddings or THIS dress budget) can far outperform a generic site-wide signup; make the CTA reflect the page.

findings.finding: Users spent about 57% of their page-viewing time above the fold and 74% in the first two screenfuls (up to 2160px).
findings.quote: In our most recent study, users spent about 57% of their page-viewing time above the fold. 74% of the viewing time was spent in the first two screenfuls , up to 2160px.
findings.context: NN/g eyetracking data (2018) on how viewing time is spread down the page; in 2010 the above-the-fold share was 80%.
findings.caveat: Viewing time, not click rate; the page itself notes the 74% can reflect short pages or people giving up. Participant count is not in the sentence.
findings.implication: A CTA placed only at the bottom of a long guide sits where little attention goes; show a CTA in the first screenful and again right after the answer.

findings.finding: 77% of couples use Pinterest for wedding inspiration (83% of Gen Z, 73% of Millennials).
findings.quote: Overall, 77% of couples use the platform for inspiration (up from 75% in 2025), driven by a massive 83% of Gen Z and 73% of Millennials.
findings.context: Zola's annual survey of couples marrying in 2026 (page last updated 2026-10-16). The 2026 sample size is not stated on the page; Zola's 2025 edition says it surveyed close to 6,000 couples.
findings.caveat: Zola's own users (a registry/website platform), self-reported; sample size not printed for 2026; Zola is now part of The Knot Worldwide family per TKWW news.
findings.implication: A bride arriving from Google already thinks in 'boards' of photos she saves; a Dream Board built by tapping photos matches an existing habit.

findings.finding: For the planning tool they find most essential, 51% of Gen Z and 45% of Millennials point to their Pinterest boards.
findings.quote: When it comes to the most essential tool in the planning process, 51% of Gen Z and 45% of Millennials still point to their Pinterest boards.
findings.context: Same Zola 2026 survey, question about the most essential planning tool.
findings.caveat: Same as above: Zola users, sample size not printed on the page; the sentence names Pinterest boards specifically.
findings.implication: The 'board' is a familiar planning object for these brides, so call the product a board, not a quiz or a profile.

findings.finding: 60% of couples say managing their actual budget against online inspiration is their number-one planning stressor, up 12% from last year.
findings.quote: In fact, 60% of couples say managing their actual budget against online inspiration is their #1 planning stressor, up 12% from last year.
findings.context: Same Zola 2026 survey; Zola frames this as the gap between what couples see online and what their budget allows.
findings.caveat: Zola users, self-reported, sample size not printed on the page; 'up 12%' is stated by Zola and not re-derived here.
findings.implication: The pain is the gap between the photos she loves and her budget, which is exactly what a board of finds 'for less' answers; lead with that gap in the CTA copy.

findings.finding: 48% of couples increased their budget or moved money around to get something they saw online (55% of Gen Z).
findings.quote: We see this play out in real spending behavior: 48% of all couples say they have increased their budget or shifted money around specifically to achieve something they saw online.
findings.context: Same Zola 2026 survey.
findings.caveat: Zola users, self-reported, no sample size on the page; it says couples spend MORE after seeing inspiration, which cuts against a pure 'save money' pitch for some brides.
findings.implication: Inspiration drives spending up; a tool that lets her keep the look while the price stays within budget speaks to the 48% who stretch.

findings.finding: 32% of couples are searching resale platforms like Poshmark for wedding attire.
findings.source_name: Zola x Poshmark 2026 Wedding Style Report
findings.quote: Secondhand goes mainstream: Nearly 1 in 3 couples (32%) are searching resale platforms like Poshmark for wedding attire, while 34% plan to incorporate a family heirloom into their look.
findings.context: Zola partnered with Poshmark to survey 800+ engaged couples (page last updated 2026-04-08); the same page also says 71% of couples are considering thrifted or pre-owned items across their wedding, from decor to signage and beyond.
findings.caveat: Co-branded with a resale marketplace that benefits from the result; n=800+; 'searching' is not 'buying'; the 71% on the same page covers decor and signage as well as attire.
findings.implication: Secondhand is a normal thing for an engaged bride to be looking at, so a secondhand-dress board does not need to apologise for being secondhand.

findings.finding: Couples say they choose vintage mainly because it feels unique (71%), meaningful (61%) and timeless (48%); cost (28%) and sustainability (27%) matter less.
findings.source_name: Zola x Poshmark 2026 Wedding Style Report
findings.quote: Style over savings: While sustainability (27%) and cost (28%) matter, couples are choosing vintage primarily because it feels more unique (71%), meaningful (61%), and timeless (48%).
findings.context: Same 800+ couple survey; reasons for choosing vintage/pre-loved items.
findings.caveat: Co-branded with Poshmark; multi-select reasons; about vintage curation generally, not specifically a dress bought on a budget.
findings.implication: Pitch the board on 'one-of-a-kind finds that fit your look' first and 'for less' second, not price alone.

findings.finding: 37% of couples contacted more vendors than they had planned in order to find options that fit their budget.
findings.source_name: The Knot Worldwide, 2026 Real Weddings Study release
findings.quote: Even amid economic pressures, 37% of couples reached out to more vendors than initially planned to find options that fit within their budget.
findings.context: Self-reported responses from 10,474 US couples married in 2025, recruited by email from The Knot and/or WeddingWire membership (stated on the same page).
findings.caveat: Company press release about its own members; self-reported; respondents are married couples recalling last year.
findings.implication: Budget-driven extra searching is common: a board that does the searching weekly saves the work she is already doing by hand.

findings.finding: Couples hire an average of 13 vendors for their wedding.
findings.source_name: The Knot Worldwide, 2026 Real Weddings Study release
findings.quote: Couples hire an average of 13 vendors to bring their day to life, reinforcing that weddings remain deeply rooted in professional expertise and human connection.
findings.context: Same 10,474-couple survey of 2025 weddings.
findings.caveat: Company press release; counts hired vendors, not hours of research (no research-hours figure was found on a credible page).
findings.implication: A bride is sourcing many categories at once, so a board that spans dresses, flowers and venues covers several of her searches in one place.

findings.finding: Nearly 90 percent of couples set their wedding budget before researching vendors and their costs, which leads to unrealistic expectations.
findings.source_name: The Knot Worldwide, Knot Budget Advisor release (Oct 2024)
findings.quote: Nearly 90 percent of couples set their wedding budget before researching vendors and their costs, leading to unrealistic expectations.
findings.context: Stated in the launch release for The Knot's Budget Advisor tool; no sample size printed on the page.
findings.caveat: Written to sell a new tool; no sample size or method on the page; 2024.
findings.implication: Brides often meet real prices only after fixing a budget, which is why a 'what does it actually cost' guide is useful and why a tool showing real finds in her price range is a natural next step.

findings.finding: In a poll of nearly 2,500 brides, 46% would be willing to consider getting married in a pre-loved gown and 54% would not.
findings.quote: A poll of nearly 2,500 Easy Weddings brides showed that 46% of brides would be willing to consider getting married in a pre-loved gown, while 54% wouldn’t hear of it.
findings.context: Reader poll on an Australian wedding directory; the page is undated.
findings.caveat: Weak: self-selected website poll, Australian, undated, 'willing to consider' not purchase; and the page also says 'over a thousand brides' in its intro, so the exact n is inconsistent.
findings.implication: Only about half of brides will entertain a pre-owned gown, so lead the board with the look and the price, and let 'preowned' appear as a fact about each find rather than the pitch.

findings.finding: Pinterest reports over 7 billion wedding-related searches and more than 16.7 billion saved wedding ideas globally in the last year.
findings.quote: last year people made over 7 billion wedding-related searches 2 and saved more than 16.7 billion wedding ideas globally.
findings.context: Pinterest's own platform counts, reported with its 2026 wedding trend report.
findings.caveat: Platform self-report of volume, not a survey of couples; says nothing about conversion or budget.
findings.implication: Saving wedding photos is a mass behaviour, so asking her to tap photos she likes is a familiar, low-effort first action.

no_evidence: A/B test with numbers, from an allowed source, of 'no credit card required' / 'free' microcopy next to a CTA (only anecdotes of +15% and +19% on vendor blogs, with no sample size; SaaS trial benchmarks compare trial models, not copy).
A published test of a time-to-complete label ('takes 90 seconds') next to a button (only survey-length studies in minutes).
ContentVerve/Aagaard privacy-line test (+19.47%) and the Delivra privacy-guarantee test (+35%): found only as secondhand mentions (CXL community page empty, no original), so not cited.

Share of informational-page readers who click any CTA, from a credible source (IMPACT's banner 0.6% / sidebar 0.2% / below-post 3.2% numbers are on a page curl cannot read; Vye and First Page Sage are vendor aggregates).
A controlled test of a topic-matched (contextual) CTA vs a generic CTA with a lift number; the HubSpot 6% vs 93% anchor-text comparison and the Backlinko content upgrade are the closest.
Calculator or tool linked from an informational article, conversion rate from a credible independent source (the only number, VenturePact +28%, sits in a vendor slide deck).
Share of brides who actually bought a secondhand wedding dress (only 'would consider' and 'searching' shares).

Share of couples who go over budget: The Knot's 53% / $7,347 overspend page returns HTTP 403 to curl and WebFetch, so it could not be opened; the older WeddingWire/Knot over-budget figures were seen only in search summaries.
Hours of vendor research per couple (a '6 hours a week' figure appeared only in a search summary with no readable source page).
notes: All 17 cited pages were read by curl and every quote was copied from the stripped page text; raw HTML is in .cache/raw/conv/r3/ (files named by sha1 of the URL, plus zero.pdf for the Ariely paper). Not cited because curl or WebFetch could not read the page: theknot.com (403), impactbnd.com (returned a listing page), impactplus.com (Cloudflare challenge), community.cxl.com/t/989 (empty), businesswire.com (empty). The Ariely entry is a fragment from a two-column PDF (it passed the verifier). Baymard's seal survey (same article as the 19% finding) says a completely homemade, meaningless seal 'performed significantly better than the SSL seals issued by established vendors except Norton', i.e. any visible reassurance icon beats none of that kind, but it prints no usable share figure in a quotable sentence. The GoodUI counts on its Patterns page change as tests are added (647 then 648 during this session), so that one quote is a snapshot. Also: the scratchpad is shared between the three researchers and researcher 2's build.py overwrote mine mid-session, so my r3.json was patched in place; if r2.json looks regenerated at about 18:31, that was my accidental run of their build script (it rewrote r2.json from their own script, no content of mine involved). Strongest tier for our decision: HubSpot 6% vs 93% (in-text link beats end banner), Zola 2026 (Pinterest boards, budget-vs-inspiration stress, unique over cheap), Backlinko page-specific offer. Everything in FRICTION is weak or indirect; no credible test isolates our exact cue. Note for the coordinator: The Knot Worldwide announced on 2026-10-14 that it will welcome Zola into its portfolio, so 'Zola' and 'Knot' figures may soon share one source.
